interactions.summary: A student says exile and isolation become bearable when intuition tells you that you are doing the right thing, even without logical proof.
Jiang reframes Dante's relief as bodily and moral knowledge that exile was not his fault, which frees him from self-blame.
A student asks why Dante could not use willpower to remain in Florence if Piccarda could maintain inward fidelity under coercion.
Jiang answers that Piccarda and Dante have different purposes: Piccarda's will aims at serving God in the convent, so her case cannot be mapped directly onto Dante's political exile.
A very brief audience acknowledgment lands between Jiang's question and his fuller answer.
Jiang says Dante's real will is not office, rule, or victory over enemies but the vocation to write the Divine Comedy and become the greatest poet in history.
A student asks whether Dante's death after finishing the poem should be read as the consequence or completion of his divinely ordered mission.
Jiang calls it a strong question and pivots to Dante's bodily condition, asking whether Dante was ever healthy at all.

speaker_notes.note: The diarization marks only a one-word response, which appears to be a minimal audience acknowledgment rather than a substantive contribution.

claims.claim: A student says intuitive moral certainty, rather than logic, explains why Dante could endure exile and isolation without collapsing.
Jiang says the crucial psychological shift is Dante's recognition that exile and isolation were not his fault.
Jiang distinguishes Piccarda from Dante by purpose: Piccarda's unwavering will is to serve God in religious life, while Dante's vocation lies elsewhere.
Jiang says Dante's will is fulfilled through writing the Divine Comedy and becoming a world-historical poet, not through ruling Florence, becoming pope, or conquering enemies.
Jiang treats Dante's health as relevant to explaining why he died after finishing the Divine Comedy rather than assuming the poem's completion was the sole cause.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang turns exile into something survivable once Dante can say, at the level of the body, that it was not his fault.
signature_moments.source_phrase: the body knows it's not his fault
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It concentrates Jiang's whole consolation reading into a single psychological release from self-accusation.

signature_moments.moment: The answer to the Piccarda objection is vocation: Dante is not meant to keep office or win politically but to write the poem history needs.
signature_moments.source_phrase: To write the Divine Comedy, guys
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It makes Jiang's account of will teleological rather than merely stubborn or activist.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang strips away every worldly ambition and leaves Dante with a single identity: the poet.
signature_moments.source_phrase: His will is to be the poet
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the packet's sharpest statement of how exile redirects Dante from politics toward authorship.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The concrete divine or personal vocation that explains why one person's use of will cannot simply be copied onto another's situation.
Jiang uses will as the deep aim organizing Dante's life, here identified with poetic vocation rather than political success.
Not merely a political punishment but a condition whose emotional burden changes when Dante stops treating it as his own fault.

chronology_notes.note: On 2026-06-17 Jiang ties Dante's release from exile-trauma to a vocation claim: innocence matters, but the larger reinterpretation is that exile serves the making of the poet who writes the Divine Comedy.

uncertainty_notes.note: The student's sentence is repetitive and rough at the transcript level, so the extraction keeps only the stable contrast between intuition and logic.
The single-word response is too thin to support a substantive claim and is treated only as a brief audience acknowledgment.
